## 8. Models

<!-- models:start (generated by tools/process_models.mjs; edit outside these markers) -->

### Retro VHS (`lumenary:retro-vhs`, models this process)

_From: Home video recorders; when: 1976 to the early 2000s; works best on: Everyday scenes, party photos and street shots._

A worn tape is a record of small mechanical failures: the picture wobbles, colours smear, a band of noise rolls up the screen and the bottom of the frame bends. Each of those flaws is simple arithmetic on lines of the picture, and together they create the feel of a memory that has been replayed too often.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Raise contrast by 12 percent and add a faint cool cast, as if the picture had been copied.
2. Shift every line sideways by the sum of two slow sine waves plus a little random jitter that changes 24 times a second.
3. Drift a tracking band down the screen, throwing lines far to the side inside it and adding dropout speckle.
4. Sample red, green and blue at slightly different horizontal positions for colour bleed.
5. Dim alternate rows, add static and corner shading, and stamp the PLAY overlay.

**The maths:**

$$\Delta x(y,t)=a_1\sin(0.05\,y+3.1\,t)+a_2\sin(0.013\,y-1.4\,t)+a_3\,\big(h(y,\text{frame})-\tfrac12\big)$$

_Horizontal shift of scanline y. The a’s scale with the distortion slider and the width._ (primitives: coordinate-warp, seeded-random)

$$\Delta x_{\text{band}}=\Big(1-\frac{\lvert y-y_c(t)\rvert}{b}\Big)^{2}\big(h-0.3\big)\,0.11\,W\,\text{dist}$$

_Extra shift inside the tracking band of half-height b whose centre y_c moves with time._ (primitives: coordinate-warp)

$$R=\tfrac12\big(S_r(x{+}c)+S_r(x{+}c{+}3)\big),\quad G=S_g(x),\quad B=S_b(x{-}c)$$

_Colour bleed: each channel sampled at its own horizontal offset c._ (primitives: misregistration)

**Dials:** `distortion` (Tracking) = 55 [0 to 100]; `noise` (Tape noise) = 40 [0 to 100]; `scan` (Scanlines) = 55 [0 to 100]; `osd` (PLAY overlay) = true.

**History:** JVC introduced VHS in Japan in 1976, and it won the format battle against Sony’s Betamax in the 1980s. Rental shops and camcorders made it the way a generation recorded birthdays, holidays and television. Each copy lost a little quality, which is why smeared colour and tracking noise now stand for nostalgia.
